summary.text: Ceyx king of Trachis sailed against his wife Alcyone's prayers to consult Apollo's oracle — and drowned in a storm crying her name; Juno sent a dream of his death, and when his body washed ashore both were changed into halcyon birds, nesting on calm winter seas while Aeolus held the winds for seven days.

chapters.title: The voyage
chapters.text: After Midas' golden touch, Ovid sings of love on the shore. Ceyx son of Lucifer reigned at Trachis without bloodshed, his face bright with his father's light; Alcyone daughter of Aeolus clung to him and begged him not to sail — the sea had taken her mother and her brothers. He would not stay; the ship put out for Claros and Apollo's oracle.

chapters.title: The storm
chapters.text: Wind and lightning broke the vessel; Ceyx had no armour but his love, and as the waves closed over him he cried Alcyone! Alcyone! — glad only that she did not share his death. Apollodorus tells a different cause for their end: he called his wife Hera and she called him Zeus, and for that hubris the king of gods turned them into birds.

chapters.title: The dream
chapters.text: Juno, pitying a wife who prayed at every altar for a husband already drowned, sent Iris to the cave of Sleep, and Morpheus stood over Alcyone in the likeness of Ceyx — pale, wet, with seawood in his hair — and told her to mourn. At dawn she ran to the shore still hoping; Hyginus instead has her leap into the sea when she learns of the wreck.

chapters.title: Halcyon days
chapters.text: She saw his body borne in on the waves and flew to meet it — then felt her arms grow wings, her lips grow narrow, and Ceyx rise beside her as a bird. Together they nested on the winter sea while Aeolus restrained his winds for seven days each year, the halcyon days when sailors know a brief calm. Love, not pride, is Ovid's reason; the birds preserve their names in both tellings.
